title: The Midnight Veil
premise: Wren Okonkwo, the youngest and most overlooked member of the Guild of Impossible Trades, discovers that the guild's ledgers record not just sales but debts owed by the world itself—and that a dying country, Veles, has been quietly erased from every map and memory except the guild's books. The child who arrives speaking Veles's pre-kingdom tongue is that country's last living anchor, and the guild's aging masters intend to sell her to the collectors who devoured Veles. Refusing to be invisible any longer, Wren steals both the child and the master ledger and flees toward the one door that still opens into the lost country, pursued by collectors wearing the faces of people she loves. In the climax Wren learns she was born in Veles herself—her invisibility was the price of her escape as an infant—and she must choose between reclaiming her erased homeland and letting it die so the child can live free; she pays her own name into the ledger to buy the child's passage, ending the book as a nameless keeper of a guild reborn around found family rather than profit.
about_author: Kestrel Kavanagh is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the property records of towns that no longer appear on maps. They write fantasy about paperwork, memory, and the quiet violence of being forgotten.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Debts
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren catalogs the guild's strangest inventory—a jar of last words, a key that fits no lock yet—while her masters dismiss her as a glorified clerk. A child arrives at the guild's door at midnight, speaking a language no living person should know. Emotional beat: the ache of being competent but unseen, and the first crack of curiosity that will undo her careful smallness.

chapters.title: A Language Older Than Kingdoms
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren secretly cross-references the child's speech against the guild's oldest ledgers and finds it matches entries from a country called Veles—a name that appears in no atlas and in no one's memory but the books. When she mentions it aloud, the masters go pale and forbid her to speak it again. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery curdling into fear.

chapters.title: What the Masters Owe
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, with a fragmentary ledger excerpt. Wren spies on a midnight meeting and learns the masters intend to sell the child to the Collectors—entities that erased Veles and are owed its remainder. She realizes the guild's wealth is built on debts like this one. Emotional beat: disillusionment; the family she served is revealed as a marketplace.

chapters.title: Theft of a Person
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren takes the child, Ilma, and the master ledger and flees through the guild's back ways, discovering Ilma can see the seams of the world—doorways Wren cannot. The Collectors arrive wearing the face of Wren's dead mother. Emotional beat: terror and a fierce, sudden protectiveness; Wren's invisibility becomes her weapon for the first time.

chapters.title: The Road That Forgets Itself
chapters.summary: Ilma's POV. Fleeing through countryside that subtly rearranges itself, Ilma navigates by the old tongue while Wren learns to trust her. They shelter with a smuggler, Odile, who once traded in Veles and remembers fragments she was paid to forget. Emotional beat: tentative found family forming between the girl, the child, and the broken woman who helps them.

chapters.title: The Price of a Name
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Reading the master ledger, Wren finds her own birth recorded: born in Veles, smuggled out as an infant, her name paid as toll to the Collectors—her lifelong invisibility is a debt, not a trait. Odile confirms it and is taken by the Collectors as punishment for helping. Emotional beat: identity shattered and rekindled; grief for Odile hardens into resolve.

chapters.title: Doors in the Water
chapters.summary: Ilma's POV. Ilma reveals the truth she couldn't say in words: she is Veles's last anchor, and if the Collectors take her, the country dies forever; if she goes home, she is bound there alone. The door out of Veles opens only once more, at the drowned harbor, at the new moon. Emotional beat: the child's loneliness mirrored against Wren's—two people erased, deciding together.

chapters.title: The Collectors' Market
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Cornered in a border town, Wren bargains with the Collectors directly, offering the ledger for Ilma's freedom. They counter with an offer she can't refuse on paper: her homeland restored, her name returned, if she hands over the child. Emotional beat: temptation at its most seductive—the chance to be seen, to belong—held against love.

chapters.title: The Door Out of Veles
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, climax. At the drowned harbor under the new moon, Wren opens the last door into Veles and learns the full truth: the country can live again only if someone with Veles blood stays and anchors it. She writes her own name into the ledger as payment, erasing herself from the Collectors' reach and freeing Ilma to walk out into the world. Emotional beat: sacrifice as self-definition—Wren chooses who she is rather than who she was told to be.

chapters.title: The Ledger Reborn
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, epilogue-like. Nameless but not gone, Wren remains Veles's anchor as the country slowly re-knits itself, while Ilma, Odile's memory, and a growing circle of the forgotten rebuild the guild as a refuge rather than a marketplace. Ilma visits through the door, bringing letters and bread and news. Emotional beat: quiet, earned hope—found family persisting across a threshold, and invisibility transformed into sanctuary.
